name: Tui na

card.summary: A traditional Chinese hands-on massage therapy used for muscle and joint complaints, which people use for recovery and comfort that can support training and posture.
card.note: Reviews describe most trials as low quality; adverse effects are possible with any manual therapy.

quick.overview:
Tui na is a form of Chinese therapeutic massage, a branch of traditional Chinese medicine, whose name means roughly push and grasp. Practitioners knead, roll, press and rub the body and sometimes combine it with acupuncture, cupping or herbal care.

The appearance link is indirect: people use it for neck and back discomfort and recovery from exercise, which can support more consistent training, comfortable posture and general upkeep. Systematic reviews of randomised trials report improvements in pain and other outcomes, with authors noting weak study quality.
quick.how: Sessions are delivered by a trained practitioner using hands-on techniques such as kneading, pressing, rolling and stretching, usually in a clinic or acupuncture practice. Athletes and exercisers are described in a sports-medicine review as increasingly interested in such traditional Chinese therapies.
quick.risks: Adverse effects are described as possible with traditional Chinese therapies in sports medicine, and in the reviewed trials of tui na few were reported. Practitioners advise against it in children with infectious disease, fractures, open wounds or bleeding disorders, and people with spinal conditions should seek medical advice.

lead: Tui na is a hands-on massage therapy within traditional Chinese medicine, comparable to shiatsu and often combined with acupuncture, moxibustion, cupping, herbs, qigong or tai chi. The Chinese name is glossed as 'push and grasp' [1].

Practitioners brush, knead, roll, press and rub the body and use range-of-motion work, traction and acupressure; paediatric tui na uses lighter strokes and spinal rolling [1]. A review of traditional Chinese therapies in sports medicine says these are used by athletes and regular exercisers for sports injuries, while stressing that adverse effects are possible and that more well-designed studies are needed [2].

Its link to looks runs through recovery, comfort and posture: people use it for muscle tightness, neck and back stiffness and post-exercise soreness, which affects how consistently they can train and how comfortably they carry themselves. Randomized trials exist for neck and back pain, insomnia, stroke spasticity and several childhood conditions [3][4][5][6][8][9].

chain: Massage of tight muscles and joints
angle.text: Tui na is used to ease muscle and joint complaints, which can make regular training and good posture easier. Any benefit to appearance comes through that recovery route.

paras: Wikipedia describes tui na as rooted in Daoist principles and aimed at restoring balance among the eight principles of traditional Chinese medicine. Practitioners brush, knead, roll, press and rub the areas between joints, called the 'eight gates', with the stated goal of opening the body's defensive qi and moving energy through the meridians and muscles [1]. Pressure ranges from gentle to firm, and other strokes include shaking and rhythmic tapping, with range-of-motion work, traction and acupressure points added by some practitioners [1].

Grokipedia lists eight foundational manipulations, namely palpating, pressing, kneading, rolling, vibrating, pulling, pushing and grasping, and says sessions typically last 30 to 60 minutes with the client clothed [7]. Proponents claim benefit for acute and chronic musculoskeletal problems and for some non-musculoskeletal conditions [1].

A branch treats infants and children, typically up to age twelve, with lighter, faster strokes concentrated on the hands, forearms, abdomen and back; common techniques include brushing along meridians, circular kneading and spinal rolling. Under traditional theory children's lung, spleen and kidney systems are delicate and still developing, and the branch is used for digestive and respiratory complaints and general wellness [1].

Grokipedia traces tui na to early Chinese manual healing, citing references to pressing and rubbing (anmo) in the Huangdi Neijing, compiled around 200 BCE, development through the Han and Tang dynasties, and use of the name tui na in Ming-dynasty paediatric massage literature [7]. It describes a revival after 1949 under state promotion of traditional Chinese medicine, with a first formal training programme in Shanghai in 1956 and a national association in 1987 [7]. Those dates come from an AI-generated encyclopedia and have not been checked against specialist histories here.
Wikipedia notes related traditions: the Korean chu na and the Japanese anma, which gave rise to shiatsu and sekkotsu, and that tui na is taught at some acupuncture schools in Western countries [1].

People who lift or play sport use manual therapies for soreness and tightness, and a sports-medicine review describes athletes and regular exercisers using traditional Chinese therapies such as tui na for sports injuries [2]. The appearance chain is indirect: less stiffness and pain can mean more consistent training, easier upright posture and a more comfortable neck and shoulder line, which people link to how they stand and move.

A systematic review of five randomized trials (448 patients) of tui na for cervical radiculopathy found lower pain scores compared with traction, with no adverse effects reported; the authors rated the supporting evidence as low or very low quality [3].

A meta-analysis of 16 randomized trials (1,502 children) on paediatric tui na for cough found pooled benefits on some outcomes, with most trials rated poor quality and certainty low [4]. A systematic review of 26 randomized trials examined paediatric tui na for acute diarrhoea in children under five against conventional treatment such as probiotics and diosmectite, using clinical cure and diarrhoea duration as primary outcomes [8]. A separate review compared tui na with the sleep medicine estazolam for insomnia [5].

A randomized clinical trial examined tui na for upper-limb spasticity after stroke [6], and a 2024 randomized comparative trial compared tui na with positional release techniques for low back pain in the third trimester of pregnancy [9]. Two trial protocols describe planned randomized studies of tui na for chronic low back pain: a 2014 protocol [10] and a protocol of a single-centre, assessor-blinded trial at Yueyang Hospital in Shanghai comparing twice-weekly tui na for 12 weeks with health education, using the Oswestry Disability Index as primary outcome [11]. The authors of that protocol note that participants and therapists cannot be blinded [11]. A China-Germany randomized trial concluded tui na may be a safe, low-cost way to reduce neck and back pain [1].

A systematic review of five randomised trials (448 patients) of tui na for cervical radiculopathy found lower pain scores compared with traction, with no adverse effects reported; the authors rated the supporting evidence as low or very low quality [3].

A meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (1,502 children) on paediatric tui na for cough found pooled benefits on some outcomes, with most trials of poor quality and low certainty [4]. A separate review compared tui na with estazolam for insomnia [5]. A Chinese-German randomised trial concluded tui na may be a safe, low-cost way to reduce back and neck pain [1].
Wikipedia's article carries a maintenance notice asking for more reliable medical references [1]. Reviews of tui na generally call for larger, better-designed trials [3][4].

Tui na sits alongside acupuncture, moxibustion, cupping, gua sha and qigong in the traditional Chinese medicine toolkit [1][2]. Reviews list tui na among external therapies described for conditions such as heat stroke [12]. Related massage traditions include shiatsu and Western sports massage [1].

The name tui na emerges in Ming-dynasty paediatric massage literature, per Grokipedia.[7]
First formal tui na training programme established in Shanghai, per Grokipedia.[7]
Chinese National Tui Na Association founded, per Grokipedia.[7]
Systematic review of tui na for cervical radiculopathy published.[3]
Randomized trial of tui na for post-stroke upper-limb spasticity published; review of tui na versus estazolam for insomnia.[6][5]
Meta-analysis of paediatric tui na for cough in children published.[4]
Randomized comparison of tui na and positional release for pregnancy-related low back pain published.[9]
